Graph-Native Infrastructure for Context and Accountable AI Systems

Developer-first, knowledge infrastructure for AI, alternative to expensive enterprise platforms.

Ingest your enterprise data, extract what matters, build a Context Graph and knowledge graph (KG), and run graph analytics and causal reasoning over all of it, with full decision provenance baked in. Explainable, traceable, and trustworthy by design.

Context Management · Knowledge Modeling · Deterministic Reasoning · Ontology Management · Decision Intelligence · End-to-End Traceability

Open Source · Governed · Zero Vendor Lock-In

Polyglot Graph Storage · RDF & LPG Support · W3C Standards · Interoperable

Built for High-Stakes, Regulated Domains

pip install semantica

English · Deutsch · Français · Español · Italiano · Português · العربية · اردو · हिन्दी · 中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Knowledge Explorer · Context Graphs · Reasoning Engine · Decision Intelligence · Ontology Hub

▶ Watch the full platform walkthrough

Most AI agents run on embeddings, not meaning: similarity scores with no structure, no relationships, and no way to explain why a result came back.

Semantica is the semantic/context layer underneath your LLM, vector store, and agent framework: deterministic infrastructure (no LLM required for graph construction, reasoning, or provenance; where an LLM is used, it's optional and vendor-neutral, every major provider supported, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and more, via semantica.llms ) that turns fragmented enterprise data into a structured, queryable Context Graph and knowledge graph that carries the business context, not just the data structure. Ontologies and controlled vocabularies (OWL, SHACL, SKOS) make what an entity means to your business, its definitions, relationships, and rules, as explicit as the data itself, not just its embedding.

Decision provenance and audit trails aren't the product. They fall out of that structure for free, and in domains a regulator can question, the same structure that makes your agent smarter also gives you a straight answer to "why."

System-level explainability, not foundation-model explainability. Semantica doesn't expose or reconstruct what happens inside the LLM: its internal reasoning stays opaque, like it does for any external system. Semantica explains what's outside the model: the context fed in, the decision produced, its provenance, relevant relationships, applied policies, and the full execution trail.

Who it's for:

AI/ML platform teams shipping agents that make consequential decisions and need structured, queryable context, not just a vector index

Enterprise data teams on Databricks, Snowflake, or SAP turning tables already in the lakehouse or warehouse into a governed, lineage-tracked knowledge graph, without exporting to a third-party SaaS

Compliance, risk, and audit teams who need a straight answer to "why did the AI do that?" in a format a regulator accepts

Regulated enterprises (finance, healthcare, legal, government, defense) that can't ship a black box or hand their data to someone else's SaaS to get one

Platform and infra engineers who want the KG, reasoning, and provenance stack self-hosted and swappable, not locked to one vendor's backend

Data and knowledge engineers building a KG from messy, multi-source data, where conflicting facts get flagged and duplicates get merged, not silently overwritten

Quick Start · Architecture · What You Get · Why Semantica · Decision Intelligence · Context Graphs · Recipe: Audit Trail · Module Reference · Integrations · CLI · Performance · Install

What Semantica Gives You

Context Graphs: A structured, queryable graph of everything your agent knows, decides, and reasons about

Decision Intelligence: Every decision is a first-class object: traceable, searchable by precedent, and causally linked

AI Governance & Ontology: SHACL constraints, conflict detection, compliance rules, OWL generation, and SKOS vocabularies, all with a visual editor

Full Auditability: W3C PROV-O provenance on every fact, exportable to JSON, CSV, or RDF

Deterministic Reasoning: Forward chaining, Rete network, Datalog, and SPARQL, with fully explainable paths, not black boxes

Knowledge Pipeline: Multi-source ingestion, entity-aware chunking, NER/relation/event extraction, and graph construction, with semantic dedup and provenance-preserving merges built in

Enterprise Data Platforms: Native connectors for Databricks (Unity Catalog + Delta Lake), Snowflake, and SAP OData, so data already in your lakehouse or warehouse becomes graph nodes with provenance, no export/import hop

Graph Analytics: Centrality, community detection, link prediction, and shortest-path queries over the graph you just built

实况照片（Live Photo） ：抖音和小红书统一由 config/base_config.py 中的 DOWNLOAD_LIVE_PHOTO 控制，默认 True ，仅在 ENABLE_GET_MEDIA 开启时生效。设为 False 后只保存静态图，普通视频下载不受影响。实况视频与静态图使用相同的原始图片序号（如 001.jpg / 001_live.mp4 ），缺失媒体时保留序号空位。这里保存的是独立图片与随附视频，不合成手机相册的 Live Photo，也不转换为 GIF。小红书 Web 返回的实况视频可能自带水印，下载会保留该视频的原始内容。

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

<a id="user-content-prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink:

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

" href="#prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness">

Documentation •

Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

The Recursive Language Model (RLM) treats context as variables ( prompt-as-a-variable ) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls ( programmatic tool /sub-agent calling ) inside a persistent REPL.

The Continual Harness stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Install the latest stable version with the one-command installer:

curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh

On Windows, install from PowerShell:

irm https: // app.primeintellect.ai / prime - agent / install.ps1 | iex

The Windows installer downloads the latest stable Windows x64 build and verifies its checksum before installation.

Why Prime Agent

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

Everything is programmatic: a persistent Python REPL is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.

Subagents are built in: rlm.spawn(...) spawns real child agents for parallel or background work and returns their results programmatically.

The harness can improve: /refine reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.

Skills can be executable: Python skills in your user configuration are imported into the kernel; repository skills provide Markdown instructions without automatic code execution.

Sessions run in the background: daemon-backed agents keep running when the terminal disconnects and can be reattached later.

Agents communicate directly: running agents can exchange messages and orchestrate one another without routing everything through the user.

Long tasks keep moving: automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous mode, and retained subagents preserve progress across turns and terminal sessions.

Getting Started

Start Prime Agent from the repository or directory you want it to work in:

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="cd /path/to/project

prime-agent"> cd /path/to/project

On first launch, run /login to choose a subscription or API-key provider. Prime Agent works in the current directory and can run commands and modify files there. Use a disposable clone, clean worktree, or another checkpoint you can inspect and restore.

Prime Agent executes model-generated Python and project commands with your user permissions. Its worker and kernel processes improve lifecycle isolation and recovery; they are not a security sandbox. Review changes and use trusted repositories, instructions, and skills only. Run untrusted code or instructions in an external sandbox or restricted environment.

Useful commands:

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="prime-agent agents # Browse running, idle, and saved sessions

prime-agent attach <agent> # Reattach to a running session

prime-agent --resume [path|id] # Browse sessions or resume one directly

prime-agent status # Inspect background service state

prime-agent doctor [--fix] # Inspect or repair background services

prime-agent update [--force] # Update Prime Agent

prime-agent shutdown [--force] # Stop every agent, worker, and background service"> prime-agent agents # Browse running, idle, and saved sessions

prime-agent attach < agent > # Reattach to a running session

prime-agent --resume [path | id] # Browse sessions or resume one directly

prime-agent status # Inspect background service state

prime-agent doctor [--fix] # Inspect or repair background services

prime-agent update [--force] # Update Prime Agent

prime-agent shutdown [--force] # Stop every agent, worker, and background service

Built for Long-Running Work

Prime Agent is built for long-running work, especially for evaluations in research. These features are available in the TUI, and when run autonomously.

Continual Harness: /refine can persist focused, reviewable lessons as supplemental prompts, memories, reusable skill descriptions, or subagent specifications, with recorded refinement history. It does not replace packaging and reviewing new executable skills.

Direct agent-to-agent communication: running agents and retained subagents can discover one another, exchange messages, and steer active work.

Daemon-backed continuity: active sessions, Python REPL state, schedules, and subagents keep running when the terminal detaches and can be reattached later.

π RuView is a WiFi sensing platform that turns radio signals into spatial intelligence.

Every WiFi router already fills your space with radio waves. When people move, breathe, or even sit still, they disturb those waves in measurable ways. RuView captures these disturbances using Channel State Information (CSI) from low-cost ESP32 sensors and turns them into actionable data: who's there, what they're doing, and whether they're okay.

What it senses:

Presence and occupancy — detect people through walls, count them, track entries and exits

Vital signs — breathing rate and heart rate, contactless, while sleeping or sitting

Activity recognition — walking, sitting, gestures, falls — from temporal CSI patterns

Environment mapping — RF fingerprinting identifies rooms, detects moved furniture, spots new objects

Sleep quality — overnight monitoring with sleep stage classification and apnea screening

Also included:

Camera-free pose — estimate 17 body keypoints from WiFi CSI

Built-in model workflow — record CSI, train models, load RVF files, and switch LoRA profiles

Local automation — HOMECORE provides state, history, automations, signed Wasm plugins, voice hooks, and HomeKit support

Unified RF world model — combine WiFi CSI, radar, UWB, and cellular sensing in one privacy-bounded scene model; accuracy is still synthetic until real-data validation

Governed evidence — attach privacy policy, uncertainty, provenance, and witness records to sensing events

The AI-Powered Life Operating System

Website · Install · Walkthrough · Docs · Releases

LifeOS-8.761.0-release.mp4

LifeOS is a General Purpose AI Harness for doing anything you want to do in life and work with AI. It captures who you are, what you care about, and where you're trying to go, then uses AI that knows you to help you get there.

And because it has your full context, it makes everything you do more efficient and effective, from building apps, to starting a business, to creative projects… basically anything .

The whole system works on one central concept: moving from your Current State to your Ideal State — in pursuit of Euphoric Surprise.

⭐ If LifeOS is useful to you, star the repo

Stars help more people find the project and keep it moving. It takes one click.

⚠️ Your Security Is Your Responsibility

LifeOS is fundamentally one person's personal AI harness, published as-is, and it is constantly in flux: security features are added, enhanced, removed, modified and adjusted from release to release. The security of any LifeOS component, and of the system as a whole, is not guaranteed. Responsibility for the security of your system is yours, not the LifeOS authors' or contributors'.

Before anything is installed, the installer asks: "Do you understand that you are responsible for the security of your own system and that we are not responsible?" It goes ahead only if you answer yes. See SECURITY.md .

Give it to your AI. LifeOS is installed by an AI, so the install is just a prompt. Paste this into your AI coding harness — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Hermes, or any capable agent — and it does the whole setup for you:

Read https://ourlifeos.ai/install and install LifeOS for me.

Your AI reads the install page and walks the setup, asking permission before it touches anything.

Prefer the terminal? There's a one-line shortcut for Claude Code on macOS/Linux:

curl -fsSL https://ourlifeos.ai/install.sh | bash

Either path needs a capable AI coding harness — we build and run on Claude Code — and bun .

Core Components

The unique features — the parts you won't find anywhere else. Anything a good harness already provides on its own (built-in subagents, for example) isn't listed; this is only what LifeOS adds. See them live and click through on ourlifeos.ai .

LifeOS ships 97 public skills, from research, security, writing and art to video, publishing and your home. Browse them all on the site.

Browse all skills →

How is LifeOS different from using an AI harness on its own?

Your harness gives you raw capability. LifeOS is the layer on top that makes it yours — a system that knows your goals, people, and context, and keeps working toward them:

Persistent memory — Your DA remembers past sessions, decisions, and learnings

Custom skills — Specialized capabilities for the things you do most

Your context — Goals, contacts, preferences—all available without re-explaining

Intelligent routing — Say "research this" and the right workflow triggers automatically

Self-improvement — The system modifies itself based on what it learns

Your harness is the engine. LifeOS is everything else that makes it your car.

What harness does LifeOS run on?

Any high-end one. LifeOS is harness-agnostic by design — it's built on universal primitives (hooks, skills, context files, agentic routing), not one vendor's features. The code is TypeScript and Bash, and the core ideas — TELOS, the Algorithm, skills, memory — port to any capable agent.

Daniel builds and runs it on Claude Code , so that's the most-tested path today. But LifeOS isn't locked to it, and it's designed to run wherever your AI does.

How is this different from fabric?

Fabric is a collection of AI prompts (patterns) for specific tasks. It's focused on what to ask AI .

LifeOS is infrastructure for how your DA operates —memory, skills, routing, context, self-improvement. They're complementary. Many LifeOS users integrate Fabric patterns into their skills.

What if I break something?

Recovery is straightforward:

Back up first — Before any upgrade: cp -r ~/.claude ~/.claude-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)

USER/ is safe — Your customizations in USER/ are never touched by the installer or upgrades

Settings merge, not overwrite — The installer only updates identity and version fields; your hooks, statusline, and custom config are preserved

Git-backed — Version control everything, roll back when needed

History is preserved — Your DA's memory survives mistakes

DA can fix it — Your DA helped build it, it can help repair it

Re-install — Run the installer again; it detects existing installations and merges intelligently

Local Model Support

Run LifeOS with local models (Ollama, llama.cpp) for privacy and cost control

Remote Access

Access your LifeOS from anywhere—mobile, web, other devices

🔥 Firecrawl

Knowledge infrastructure to make your agents smarter. 🔥 You can use Firecrawl three ways. This repo holds the code for Firecrawl Local and the self-hosted server, along with SDKs that work with all three.

Firecrawl Local . Run Firecrawl on your own machine as one binary that turns websites into clean markdown, plugs into your AI agent as an MCP server and serves the Firecrawl API on localhost.

Firecrawl Cloud . Use the hosted service at firecrawl.dev for everything Local does at scale with nothing to run, plus search and the 550+ data providers in Firecrawl Alexandria for far more knowledge than scraping alone.

Self-hosting . Deploy the full Firecrawl server from apps/api with its own queues, workers and databases on your own infrastructure.

Pst. Hey, you, join our stargazers :)

Firecrawl Local

Firecrawl Local scrapes, crawls and maps from your own machine without a database, queue or container, and it reaches Firecrawl Cloud when your AI agents need search or Alexandria. It installs from crates.io. You need Rust and a C compiler, which on macOS means xcode-select --install and on Debian or Ubuntu means build-essential .

cargo install firecrawl-local

If you don't have Rust, Firecrawl Cloud runs the same scrape with nothing to build and no signup.

npx -y firecrawl-cli@latest scrape https://firecrawl.dev

Scrape a page and print its markdown.

firecrawl-local scrape https://firecrawl.dev --markdown

Crawl a site and save one markdown file per page.

firecrawl-local crawl https://docs.firecrawl.dev --limit 50 --out ./pages

List every URL on a site.

firecrawl-local map https://firecrawl.dev

Pages that need JavaScript render in the Chrome or Chromium already on your machine, and PDFs and Office documents are parsed locally too. Without a browser, static pages still work and a page that needed one comes back with a warning.

Add it to your AI agent

init finds Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Gemini CLI and Codex on your machine and adds Firecrawl Local to each one as an MCP server. It backs up every config file first, and the MCP server itself needs Node.js 22 or newer.

firecrawl-local init

Restart your AI tool afterwards. Its scrape, crawl, map and batch scrape tools run on your machine, and the other Firecrawl tools go to Firecrawl Cloud.

Run the Firecrawl API on localhost

serve answers the Firecrawl v2 API on port 3002, so code written for Firecrawl runs against it unchanged and local routes need no API key.

firecrawl-local serve

Point any Firecrawl SDK at it by setting the API URL.

<div class="highlight highlight-source-python notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="from firecrawl import Firecrawl

print(app.scrape("https://firecrawl.dev").markdown)"> from firecrawl import Firecrawl

print ( app . scrape ( "https://firecrawl.dev" ). markdown )

The Firecrawl Local README covers every command and option, the security defaults for serve and running it in Docker. Move to Firecrawl Cloud when you need structured JSON, Interact, the Agent or scale beyond one machine.

What runs where

Interact , Agent and Monitor

Scraping, crawling and mapping run on your machine. By default a single-page scrape that won't load there is fetched by Firecrawl Cloud instead and marked "source": "firecrawl-cloud" in the result. Those Cloud calls work without an account at a limited rate, and firecrawl-local login puts them on your Firecrawl account. Set FIRECRAWL_CLOUD=off to keep everything on your machine.

Firecrawl Cloud

Firecrawl Cloud runs everything Firecrawl Local does at scale, with no browser or machine of your own to look after. It also gives your AI agents access to far more knowledge than scraping alone, with search, Alexandria, Interact and Agent all through a single API.

Works on the real web. Covers 96% of the web, including JS-heavy pages and dynamic apps ( see benchmarks ).

WeatherNext 2

This repo contains the code for WeatherNext 2 (WN2), the global, medium-range

atmospheric and cyclone forecasting model developed by Google DeepMind and

Google Research.

It also contains code for prior generation models

Accessing Forecast Data Feeds

If you are interested in directly accessing daily data feeds of WN2 model

outputs rather than running the model yourself, we provide them across multiple

Google Cloud

(including Earth Engine, BigQuery, and Vertex AI).

WeatherLab (including cyclone tracks).

OpenMeteo (including an API and interactive builder).

Model Guide & Documentation: Google Developers WeatherNext Guide

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper: Operational tropical cyclone forecasting

FGN/WN2 Technical Report: Skillful joint probabilistic weather

forecasting from marginals

(arXiv:2506.10772)

WeatherNext 2 Blog Post: WeatherNext 2: Our most advanced weather forecasting model

WeatherNext Cyclones Blog Post: WeatherNext: AI model achieves breakthrough in forecasting cyclones

Older Models

This repository serves as the primary home for the WeatherNext family models.

Alongside WN2, this repository also hosts the code and documentation for our

legacy and specialized models:

WeatherNext Graph : Deterministic

medium-range weather forecasting using graph neural networks. Published as

WeatherNext Gen : Diffusion-based ensemble

forecasting for medium-range weather. Published as GenCast.

Provided Pretrained Models

This repository provides code to run the different versions of WeatherNext 2 and

WeatherNext Cyclones. The only difference between them is that WN2 can also

predict 100m wind. In particular, WN2 also forecasts cyclones with the exact

same algorithm as WN Cyclones. Their weights are different due to independent

training runs.

WeatherNext 2

WeatherNext2_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution (~30km).

Fine-tuned on ECMWF HRES data and designed to be initialized directly from

operational HRES initial conditions rather than ERA5 reanalysis. Trained on

data through 2024. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNext2_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones - models which reproduce the results in paper

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution. The

model that ran live during the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, publicly

referred to as FNV3 (NHC's postprocessed version was called GDMI). Trained

on data through 2024. The paper appendix contains a partial evaluation of

2025 in NHC basins for this model checkpoint, and how the tracker

improvement in September 2025 improved results. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2024. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2023. Trained on data through 2022. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones Mini

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024 : 1° resolution. A lightweight version

suitable for lower memory and compute constraints (e.g., local testing or

single TPUs or GPUs). Not expected to match the performance of the larger

versions. Forecasts the same things as WeatherNext2_<2025, including

cyclones. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights file:

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023 : As above, but only trained on data through

2022. Corresponding weights file: WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023.npz .

Evaluation results for WeatherNextCyclones_Mini can be found in the appendix

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper .

Quick Start Guide

The easiest way to get started with WeatherNext 2 is by running our interactive

Colab Notebook , which can be opened from

Colaboratory .

This notebook defaults to WeatherNext Cyclones Mini, which we recommend running

using the v5e-1 runtime, available for free as a Colab runtime. However, the

notebook can also be used to run the other models enumerated above (but these

will require a v5p accelerator).

In general, we recommend running WeatherNext 2 on TPU where possible, since its

implementation has been optimised for it. However, if choosing to run on GPU,

the attention implementation must be switched, as shown in the demo notebook.

The non-Mini models require H100 for sufficient VRAM. The Mini models should

manage inference on a P100.

Pre-trained weights and sample data are available on our Google Cloud

Inside the notebook, you will learn how to:

Automatically load the required model weights from our storage bucket.

Load initial state weather data (e.g., HRES initial conditions).

Initialize the WN2 (FGN) architecture.

Run auto-regressive rollout steps to generate a forecast prediction.

Visualize the outputs (e.g., temperature, wind speed, geopotential height).

Run the direct tracker on model outputs to obtain track data for cyclones.

Compute the training loss on model predictions and targets, and take a

gradient step.

Installation

This is research code provided as-is for the purpose of running and

experimenting with the published models. There are no guarantees of API

stability and future updates may introduce breaking changes without notice. We

recommend pinning to a specific release.

pip install git+https://github.com/google-deepmind/weathernext.git@v0.3.0

Model Weights

To run WeatherNext 2 or WeatherNext Cyclones, you will need to download the

pre-trained model weights. You can access the weights on Google Cloud

Code-Graph-RAG

Code-Graph-RAG parses a multi-language codebase with Tree-sitter, sharpened by compiler-grade frontends and runtime traces where available, builds a knowledge graph of its structure in an embedded graph database that needs no server, and lets you query, edit, and optimise that code in plain English. It works across a monorepo of mixed languages under one unified graph schema.

1. Index: cgr start --update-graph parses a repository into a knowledge graph (sped up)

2. Ask: cgr start answers questions and edits code, grounded in that graph

Latest News 🔥

Security Fix : Addressed a potential issue with parameter defaults.

Stack Handling : Improved stack management for Qdrant and Memgraph.

See NEWS.md for the full history.

What It Does

Point Code-Graph-RAG at a repository and it reads every source file, extracts functions, classes, methods, modules, and the relationships between them, and stores the result as an interconnected graph. Once the graph exists you can:

Ask questions about the codebase in natural language and get answers grounded in the real structure.

Retrieve the actual source of any function, class, or method by name or by intent.

Edit code through the agent with AST-based surgical patching and a diff preview before anything changes.

Optimise code against language best practices or your own coding standards.

Find dead code by walking call and reference edges from entry points.

Search and rewrite structurally by AST pattern with ast-grep.

Overlay runtime behaviour: trace a test run (or pull production eBPF profiles) with cgr trace and merge the calls that actually happened into the graph, exposing dispatch that static analysis cannot see.

How It Works

The system has two components:

Multi-language parser. A Tree-sitter based parser reads the codebase and ingests functions, classes, methods, modules, and their relationships into the graph under a single language-agnostic schema. Where a toolchain is available, compiler-grade frontends layer exact facts on top (libclang for C/C++, go/types for Go, and opt-in Roslyn, javac and Jedi for C#, Java and Python), and dynamic tracing merges calls observed at runtime. Tree-sitter stays the backbone: a trace only sees code that ran, and a compiler frontend only covers what its toolchain can build.

RAG system ( codebase_rag/ ). An interactive CLI that turns natural language into Cypher queries, retrieves matching code, and drives AI-powered editing and optimisation.

The graph is stored in an embedded SQLite file by default. Memgraph and Neo4j are opt-in backends that run the same Cypher; Graph Backends compares them.

Python, TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Lua, Dart, and Julia are fully supported. The open-source control plane for coding agents.

T3 Code runs the coding agents on your machine and gives them one fast interface. Start a thread at your desk, then approve the next step from your phone.

It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Antigravity, Kiro, Pi, Muse Code, fx, and any ACP agent. If an agent is set up on your computer, T3 Code can control it.

What you get

Your subscriptions. T3 Code does not resell tokens. It drives the agents you are already signed in to.

Every agent in one place. Change models in the middle of a thread. Let Claude hand a task to Codex.

Desktop, web, and phone. One server, and every client shows the same threads. There are apps for iOS and Android.

Remote ready. Run agents on any machine. Connect over your local network, Tailscale, or T3 Connect .

Git built in. Each thread can work in its own worktree. Review the diff, then commit, push, and open a pull request with one button.

Fast. Performance is a feature here. We measure it, and we treat a dropped frame as a bug.

Open. MIT licensed. If you don't like something, fork it.

Download T3 Code for macOS, Windows, or Linux. You can also use a package manager:

brew install --cask t3-code

winget install T3Tools.T3Code or scoop install extras/t3code

yay -S t3code-bin

nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

Command line

This installs the t3 command. Run t3 to start the server and open the web app.

curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

To try it once without an install, run npx t3@latest .

Get the app from the App Store or Google Play . Then follow remote access to connect it to your computer.

Sign in to an agent

T3 Code needs one agent that is installed and signed in. For example, install Claude Code and run claude auth login , or install Codex CLI and run codex login .

Provider setup has the steps for each agent. Install T3 Code covers nightly builds, AppImage, WSL, and NixOS.

"Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the tool that you want.

The most powerful and modular AI engine for content creation.

ComfyUI is the AI creation engine for visual professionals who demand control over every model, every parameter, and every output. Its powerful and modular node graph interface empowers creatives to generate images, videos, 3D models, audio, and more...

ComfyUI natively supports the latest open-source state of the art models.

It is by far the most optimized inference engine for diffusion models in the world with a focus on local consumer hardware.

Can run even the biggest open source models on as low as 4GB vram + 8GB ram relatively quickly (saturating your GPU compute) using our state of the art asynchronous weight streaming technology.

Partner nodes provide access to the best closed source models such as Nano Banana, Seedance, Hunyuan3D, etc.

It is available on Windows, Linux, and macOS, locally with our desktop application , our portable install or on our cloud .

The most sophisticated workflows can be exposed through a simple UI thanks to App Mode.

It integrates seamlessly into production pipelines with our API endpoints.

Desktop Application

The easiest way to get started.

Available on Windows & macOS.

Manual Install

Our official paid cloud version for those who can't afford local hardware.

Reusable subgraphs, workflow templates, App Mode, and a local API for integrating workflows into applications.

Efficient local execution with asynchronous queueing, partial graph re-execution, smart VRAM and RAM management, model offloading, and support for quantized models.

Broad native model support. This is a representative list; browse the workflow library for maintained, ready-to-run templates.

Image generation : Stable Diffusion 1.5, SDXL, SD3.5, Flux.1, Flux.2, Qwen Image, Z-Image, Hunyuan Image 2.1, HiDream, Lumina Image 2.0, Chroma, Anima, LongCat Image, Ideogram 4, Krea 2, MageFlow, Microsoft Lens, PixelDiT, Kandinsky 5, Ernie Image and Moss Image.

Audio and video generation : MiniMax H3 and LTX-AV.

3D and vision : Hunyuan3D 2.1, TripoSplat, SeedVR2, SUPIR, Depth Anything 3, MoGe, SAM 3 and 3.1, RT-DETRv4, and BiRefNet.

Built-in tools for inpainting, outpainting, reference conditioning, masks and compositing, model merging, upscaling, frame interpolation, segmentation, depth estimation, and media processing.

Save and load workflows as JSON, or recover complete workflows and seeds from supported generated media.

Support for saving and loading HDR videos and images in various formats.

Release Process

ComfyUI follows a weekly release cycle targeting Monday but this regularly changes because of model releases or large changes to the codebase. There are three interconnected repositories:

ComfyUI Core

Releases a new major stable version (e.g., v0.7.0) roughly every 2 weeks.

Starting from v0.4.0 patch versions will be used for fixes backported onto the current stable release.

Minor versions will be used for releases off the master branch.

Issue body actions

At 0e0c5a8 , ReleaseExposureService.close() can skip later cleanup callbacks. Its aggregate can also retain a stale resource after the child that owned it has confirmed release.

Reproduction

Make the desktop owner's close callback throw synchronously. Call service.close(). It rejects with that error, but neither the Go nor the Rust reader's close callback is called.

Have the desktop and Go owners reject with separate ProviderCleanupErrors. Let the first owner's release finish before the second close settles. The returned aggregate lists both roots, including the already released desktop root. A completed child and an opaque rejection currently take the same branch.

All callbacks are supplied through the service's existing owner interface. No external providers or real targets are required.

Expected outcome

Shutdown attempts all the owners. A single failure retains its identity. An aggregate of known cleanup owners reports the remaining resources and finishes when the last owner releases. A rejection that never supplied cleanup authority should stay unconfirmed.

Verification

Windows 11 x64, Node.js 24.22.1 and Vitest 5.0.3. Both added service-level regressions failed on the unchanged implementation. The later callback was called zero times in the first case. The second case reported both desktop-root and go-root when only go-root remained.

items.title: How to Earn a Bad Obituary
items.summary: How to Earn a Bad Obituary（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
At 79, I just walked away from being a Fellow at Google, a large, generous, well-established corporation with brilliant colleagues working on one of the most exciting chapters in computer science history. I took a pay cut to join Laude Institute — a tiny, recent nonprofit whose longevity depends on philanthropy — as a member of technical staff working with people less than half my age.

What was I thinking???

My explanation is the fifth in my series of “bad advice” pieces of my career — How to Give a Bad Talk (1983), How to Have a Bad Career (1994), How to Build a Bad Center (2013), and How to Give AI a Bad Carbon Footprint (2025) — where I give tongue-in-cheek commandments for how to do something badly and then show how to do it well. This time it’s earning a bad obituary.

Here are the four Bad Obituary Commandments:

Play it safe . You never know what will happen with the economy, so pick the path with the greatest employment safety.

Retire and relax, you’ve earned it . Why keep working if you don’t have to?

Don’t embarrass yourself . Ours is a young person’s field. Working with much younger people may expose your weaknesses and damage your reputation. Bill Belichick is a cautionary tale .

Choose wealth . The winner in life is the one with the most trailing zeros in the bank account. Elon Musk is the shining exemplar .

Following all four greatly increases your chances of earning a bad obituary!

The legend of Alfred Nobel shows the impact of a bad obituary. When his brother died in 1888, a newspaper mistook the death for Alfred’s and ran an obituary calling the inventor of dynamite a “merchant of death” who got rich helping people kill each other faster. That is, he earned a bad obituary . Shaken by how he would be remembered, the story goes, Nobel rewrote his legacy: his will funded prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. He died in 1896, with the first Nobel prizes awarded in 1901. Today, his name is known for those prizes more than for dynamite.

Nobel got his wake-up call by accident. Stephen Covey, in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People , suggests we get ours on purpose: imagine your own funeral and ask what you would want the people there to say about you. Similarly, David Brooks suggests maximizing “eulogy virtues,” like being kind, brave, honest, faithful, and loving . In short, steer clear of a bad obituary!

Here is my advice on how to avoid one:

Play it safe ? It’s actually hard to know in our fast moving field what is really the safest path in the long run. As Helen Keller put it: “Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. The fearful are caught as often as the bold.”

Retire and relax, you’ve earned it ? My mother is 99 years old, and studies suggest children of centenarians have lower mortality . Do I really want to spend 20 years as a couch potato? I’m actually more concerned about dementia than longevity. Following a quote often attributed to George Bernard Shaw: “You don’t stop playing because you grow old; you grow old because you stop playing.” I still have fire in the belly, I’m still a good problem solver, I like learning new ideas, and I have wisdom to share. And I’m still playing soccer. Working, learning, and playing are associated with lower odds of dementia, so why stop now?

Don’t embarrass yourself ? An old man trying to act like young people is a cliché, but I don’t believe that warning applies to work. (In case you were worried about a “late life” crisis, I’m still married to my high school sweetheart; next year is our 60th anniversary.) My favorite work activity is helping teams win , and I believe I can help Laude Institute win. I’ve got 50 years of relevant experience; younger colleagues can learn from me while I learn from them.

Choose wealth? My view is that becoming the richest person in the cemetery is not the right goal. I’m on record that when given the choice, I chose happiness over wealth . When psychologists study happy people, they’ve found that one key characteristic is helping others . Hence, to maximize happiness, I expected that after Berkeley I would join a nonprofit that helps the less fortunate. I searched and found many well-meaning organizations, but either they weren’t making a real dent on their problem or my participation would not actually help them move the needle. Hence, after retiring from Berkeley in 2016, I joined Google instead.

Andy Konwinski, a former student in one of my research labs and cofounder of Databricks and Perplexity , approached me in 2024 about helping academics reduce the downsides and increase the upsides of AI. Our chat led to the vision paper “ Shaping AI’s Impact on Billions of Lives ,” which evolved into the Moonshots program, a flagship initiative of Laude Institute . Laude Institute was founded to help computer scientists do high-impact open science research, with me as the founding chair of the board. I call it a public good startup : a small, scrappy, young staff working hard to achieve an ambitious, meaningful goal, with the urgency of a startup and public good as its aim.

Since then I’ve volunteered part time to guide Moonshots // One . This research competition asked today’s most consequential AI researchers a simple question: if you had the resources, how would you use AI to solve humanity’s hardest problems? Laude received 125 proposals from 600+ accomplished academics at nearly 50 great North American institutions aimed at moonshots evaluated by an all-star program committee .

items.title: Show HN: erXos – a microkernel OS in Erlang based on Genera/Plan 9/QNX ideas
items.summary: What if every Erlang process were an operating-system process? With as much system code and drivers written in Erlang itself. This is something I was pondering …
items.content:
What if every Erlang process were an operating-system process?

erXos is an operating system built on that idea. Its

drivers, file systems and services are Erlang processes, supervised and

isolated by a small capability microkernel, and its shell

feels like UNIX.

___ _ __ \ \/ / ___ ___

/ _ \| '__| \ / / _ \ / __|

| __/| | / \ | (_) |\__ \

\___||_| /_/\_\ \___/ |___/

development build: trusted code only

Erlang/OTP 29 [erts-17.1.1] [source] [64-bit] [smp:1:1] [ds:1:1:10] [async-threads:1]

rc: the command shell; erl starts the Erlang shell

% # The command shell runs rc's language, written in Erlang.

% echo hello from erXos > /tmp/hi

% cat /tmp/hi

hello from erXos

% # How many processes run? Each is an Erlang process.

% ps | wc -l

Eshell V17.1.1 (type help(). for help)

% Crash a process that divides by zero, and catch it

% with a monitor. The shell carries on.

1> {_, R} = spawn_monitor(fun() -> 1 / list_to_integer("0") end).

=ERROR REPORT==== 1-Jan-1970::00:00:02.651025 ===

Error in process <0.150.0> with exit value:

{badarith,[{erlang,'/',[1,0],[{error_info,#{module => erl_erts_errors}}]}]}

{<0.150.0>,#Ref<0.3910384898.1.60465>}

2> receive {'DOWN', R, _, _, {E, _}} -> {crashed, E} end.

{crashed,badarith}

% A ring of N processes passes a token round it Laps times.

3> Ring = fun(N, Laps) ->

.. Last = lists:foldl(fun(_, Next) ->

.. spawn(fun Loop() -> receive 0 -> Next ! 0;

.. T -> Next ! T - 1, Loop() end end)

.. end, self(), lists:seq(1, N)),

.. Alive = erlang:system_info(process_count),

.. Last ! N * Laps,

.. (fun Wait() -> receive 0 -> ok;

.. T -> Last ! T - 1, Wait() end end)(),

.. {Alive, N * Laps}

#Fun<erl_eval.41.130099583>

% 5,000 processes alive at once, 100,000 messages.

4> Ring(5000, 20).

{5061,100000}

Recorded session

At the % prompt, try ls / , top , dmesg , ifconfig , ping -c 3 8.8.8.8 , or erl for the Erlang shell.

Drivers, file systems and system services are Erlang

processes, supervised like any other. When one crashes, its supervisor

restarts it.

The machine stays open. From an Erlang shell you inspect, trace and

change it, all the way down to kernel objects. That is the goal, and

the design is built around it: a kernel that knows nothing of Erlang,

and an Erlang system that runs the machine.

In erXos, Erlang's process is the operating system's

process: one process space, one message system and one view of

identity, supervision and inspection span every runtime.

Secure by construction

Authority is a capability someone handed you. Knowing a pid, a

path or a node name grants nothing.

Millions of processes

Erlang processes are cheap to create and cheap to switch. erXos

keeps them cheap.

Crashes are routine

A driver wedges its device. It fails alone, its supervisor

restarts it, and the machine carries on.

A live machine

Upgrade a driver in place. Follow any process to the line of

source it is executing.

One kernel, many runtimes

The kernel hands out CPU time. ERTS comes first. C programs share

the machine on the same terms.

Cross-platform

AArch64 on QEMU first, then the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5. Other

architectures are ports, not redesigns.

Erlang wherever practical

Erlang runs the drivers, the file systems, the network stack and

the shell. C is for the kernel, device shims and per-byte work.

Practical is the key word.

Beauty and simplicity

A few concepts, used everywhere. A little speed is a fair price for

a lot of simplicity.

Declarative where it simplifies

One manifest says what the machine runs. The build checks it. Where

a description is simpler than code, it replaces the code.

UNIX look and feel

Shell, files, pipes, ps . FreeBSD programs, recompiled

from source. UNIX is how the system looks, not what it is built

The kernel knows threads, memory, capabilities and interrupts. It

knows nothing of Erlang. Everything else runs in user mode, the

runtimes included.

A domain is an address space with its own runtime. It is also an

Erlang node. Processes in different domains link, monitor and message

each other as Erlang processes always have. A crashed domain looks

like a dead node.

UNIX shell · files · pipes · terminals

System domain ERTS · domain service · console · services

Network domain ERTS · network drivers · TCP/IP stack

Storage domain ERTS · storage drivers · file systems

Domain ERTS · your Erlang application

Domain ERTS · another application, isolated from the first

Domain native programs on musl

liberx the kernel interface, one ABI for every runtime

user mode ↑ · ↓ kernel mode

Capability microkernel threads · memory · capabilities · interrupts · CPU grants

AArch64 QEMU virt · Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 to follow

Two-level scheduling

The kernel grants CPU time. Each runtime schedules its own

processes within that grant, without a kernel call.

A budget for everything

Every kernel allocation is charged to a budget. Delete the

budget, and everything charged to it goes too.

Private namespaces

Straight from Plan 9. There is no global root, so a path is the

visible face of a capability.

erXos stands on the shoulders of giants. Erlang/OTP gave it

processes and supervision; L4 and Fiasco, the kernel; Plan 9,

namespaces and files; QNX, UNIX on a microkernel; Genera, a whole

machine open to inspection. What is new is how the pieces meet.

Phase 1: erXos runs on a modified Fiasco behind erXos's own kernel

interface; erXos's own kernel replaces it in Phase 2.

ON QEMU virt AArch64, on 1 to 8 CPUs.

ON Raspberry Pi 4 Boots from an SD card, with Ethernet, HDMI and a serial console.

ON In the browser The console above, on an AArch64 emulator.

ON Domains Storage, network, display and each session run their own Erlang runtime, in user mode.

ON Drivers in Erlang Console, virtio block, net, gpu and input, and the Pi's SD card, Ethernet and framebuffer.

ON Network A TCP/IP stack in Erlang, with DHCP, HTTPS and SSH.

ON Graphics Windows, Plan 9's draw protocol and LVGL widgets; the kiosk shows live quotes.

ON Files Private namespaces, littlefs on /data , and EROFS checked by dm-verity.

ON Shell rc, written in Erlang, with job control and pipes.

ON Inspector Processes, domains and kernel objects at /proc .

Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program

Influencers are now able to link their Amazon and Instagram accounts to promote products. Some are concerned about what they’re opting in to.

Influencers are now able to link their Amazon and Instagram accounts to promote products. Some are concerned about what they’re opting in to.

Nov 19, 2026, 7:12 PM UTC

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge

Mia Sato is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits.

The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to.

In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads.

The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads.

Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads.

Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook , and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing .

NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.

The moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.

These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.

Starship challenges

For Starship, the evolved plan has SpaceX fueling a Starship lunar lander in low-Earth orbit before docking with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew will fly to the Moon on board Orion before two of the four astronauts transfer into Starship for a landing on the Moon.

Due to the docking configuration with Starship, Orion must now fly backward to the Moon, with its Service Module at the top of the stack. This is a fundamentally different flying posture than Orion was designed for, Shireman said, and creates issues for Orion’s propulsion system.

As a result, the Service Module, which is provided by the European Space Agency, will require modifications to its propellant tanks. This is because liquid propellant would move toward the gas inlet side of the tanks, rather than settling in the direction expected during normal operation.

“When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,” Shireman said. “Bad things can happen to you.” To address this, he said, the European Space Agency and its main contractor, Airbus, are modifying the vehicle’s tanks for Starship lunar missions.

class="my-2.5 mx-auto px-[15px] sm:px-5 lg:grid lg:max-w-5xl lg:grid-cols-3 lg:gap-6 lg:px-8 xl:px-0">

NASA and Lockheed engineers have also been studying the impact of increased acceleration on Orion when the vehicle is attached to Starship. Under Orion’s original mission architecture, the spacecraft would experience accelerations of about 0.1 to 0.15 g during the translunar injection burn, Shireman said. But with Starship providing the thrust, the acceleration would increase to approximately 0.8 to 1 g, acting in the opposite direction from the one originally planned.

Orion’s structure must be certified to handle a substantially higher acceleration in the opposite direction, Shireman said.

Artemis III concerns

Before astronauts land on the Moon, NASA is also planning a mission in low-Earth orbit to test Orion’s interactions with the lunar landers. Shireman said this change in plans for Artemis III, announced earlier this year, has created new hazards, as Orion was not designed to spend more than a short period of time in low-Earth orbit.

Heating is a concern, he said, because Orion was designed for deep space, which is colder than the thermal environment closer to Earth. For example, he said, Orion has passive thermal features designed to prevent the spacecraft from getting too cold in deep space. One of these is a silver-looking exterior tape that dissipates electrical charge and limits the radiation of heat into space. As a result, some of this tape will be removed for the Artemis III mission.

Engineers are also analyzing how to manage electrical loads to reduce heating and protect the avionics and crew cabin.

Another big change that stems from spending approximately two weeks in low-Earth orbit is the orbital debris environment, which is more congested than in deep space. Shireman said NASA and Lockheed have not completed their assessment of the orbital-debris risk associated with the new mission profile. This should be done by January, and, if the risks are too high, it might lead to modifications of Orion’s orbit for the mission.
